topics.title: C1.1 How has the Earth's atmosphere changed over time, and why?

subtopics.title: Particle model and changes of state

outcomes.text: Explain the particle model for states of matter and change of state, and tell physical from chemical changes.
Explain the limits of the particle model when particles are drawn as inelastic spheres.
Use energy transfers and the strength of forces between particles to explain why changes of state occur at different temperatures.
Use data to predict the state of a substance under given conditions.
Interpret the evidence for how the early atmosphere formed.
Describe how an oxygen-rich atmosphere developed over time.
Describe the sources of carbon monoxide, particulates, sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides.
Explain the problems these pollutants cause and how catalytic converters, low-sulfur petrol and gas scrubbers cut emissions.
Write formulae of elements and simple covalent compounds from chemical symbols.
Write balanced chemical equations using conservation of mass.
Use arithmetic and ratios when balancing equations.
Describe tests for oxygen, hydrogen and carbon dioxide.
Explain oxidation as gain of oxygen.

topics.title: C1.2 Why are there temperature changes in chemical reactions?

outcomes.text: Tell endothermic from exothermic reactions by the temperature change of the surroundings.
Draw and label reaction profiles for both, showing activation energy.
Explain activation energy as the energy needed for a reaction to occur.
Interpret charts and graphs of reaction profiles.
Describe how to investigate whether a reaction is endothermic or exothermic.
Calculate energy changes from bond breaking and bond making energies.
Carry out the arithmetic for energy change calculations.
Recall that a chemical cell gives a potential difference until the reactants are used up.
Evaluate advantages and disadvantages of hydrogen/oxygen and other fuel cells for given uses.

topics.title: C1.3 What is the evidence for climate change, why is it occurring?

outcomes.text: Describe the greenhouse effect as radiation interacting with matter.
Evaluate evidence for human causes of climate change, such as carbon dioxide rising with fossil fuel use, and its uncertainties.

subtopics.title: Effects and mitigation of climate change

outcomes.text: Describe effects of more carbon dioxide and methane: crop regions, extreme weather, melting ice and flooding.
Describe how these effects may be reduced, weighing scale, risk and environmental impact.
Extract and interpret information from charts, graphs and tables.
Use orders of magnitude to judge the significance of data.

topics.title: C1.4 How can scientists help improve the supply of potable water?

outcomes.text: Describe the main ways to increase potable water: filtration, membrane filtration, aeration, chlorination and distillation of salt water.
Describe a test for chlorine using blue litmus paper.

topics.title: C2.1 How have our ideas about atoms developed over time?

outcomes.text: Describe how and why the atomic model changed, from Dalton through Thomson and Rutherford to Bohr.
Describe the atom as a small, positive nucleus holding most of the mass, surrounded by electrons.
Recall relative charges and masses of protons, neutrons and electrons.
Estimate and recall the size and scale of atoms and small molecules.
Relate atomic size and scale to objects in the physical world.
Work out numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons from atomic and mass numbers or the Periodic Table.

topics.title: C2.2 What does the Periodic Table tell us about the elements?

outcomes.text: Explain how an element's position relates to its electron arrangement and atomic number.
Describe how Mendeleev organised elements by properties and relative atomic mass.
Describe how new elements and atomic number ordering supported Mendeleev's gaps and reordering.
Describe metals and non-metals and explain differences in their physical and chemical properties.
Recall simple properties of Group 1 elements, including reactions with moist air, water and chlorine.
Recall simple properties of Group 7 elements, including states, colours, reactions with Group 1 and displacement reactions.
Predict reactions and reactivity of elements from their position in the Periodic Table.
Describe experiments showing the reactivity pattern of Group 7, including displacement.
Describe experiments showing the reactivity pattern of Group 1 elements.

topics.title: C2.3 How do metals and non-metals combine to form compounds?

outcomes.text: Recall simple properties of Group 0, including low melting and boiling points and lack of reactivity.
Explain properties of Groups 1, 7 and 0 from their outer shell electrons and predict trends.
Explain how reactions of elements relate to their electron arrangement.
Explain how the atomic structure of metals and non-metals relates to their Periodic Table position.
Describe the nature and arrangement of bonds in ionic compounds.
Explain ionic bonding as electron transfer and electrostatic attraction.
Work out protons, neutrons and electrons in atoms and ions.
Draw dot and cross diagrams for simple ionic substances.

subtopics.title: Properties and models of ionic compounds

outcomes.text: Explain how bulk properties of ionic materials relate to their bonds.
Use energy transfers and attraction strength to explain melting points of ionic compounds compared with other bonding.
Describe limitations of dot and cross diagrams and 3-D models of ionic compounds.
Translate between diagrams and numbers, and between 2-D and 3-D representations of ionic structures.

topics.title: C2.4 How are equations used to represent chemical reactions?

outcomes.text: Write formulae of elements and simple covalent and ionic compounds from symbols.
Use the formulae of common ions to deduce Group 1 and Group 7 compound formulae.
Write formulae and balanced equations using the first 20 elements, Groups 1, 7 and 0 and other common elements.
Use state symbols (s, l, g, aq) for reactants and products.

topics.title: C2.5 What are the properties of the transition metals? (separate science only)

outcomes.text: Recall general properties of transition metals (melting point, density, reactivity, coloured ions, catalysis) with examples such as copper, iron, chromium, silver and gold.

units.title: Chapter C3: Chemicals of the natural environment

topics.title: C3.1 How are the atoms held together in a metal?

outcomes.text: Describe the nature and arrangement of bonds in metals.
Explain how bulk properties of metals relate to their bonds.

topics.title: C3.2 How are metals with different reactivities extracted?

outcomes.text: Deduce a reactivity order from reactions with water, dilute acid and displacement.
Explain metal reactivity with water or acid by how readily the metal forms its positive ion.
Write formulae, balanced equations and ionic equations for metal reactions.
Use carbon's place in the reactivity series to explain industrial extraction, including zinc.
Explain why electrolysis extracts some metals from their ores.
Evaluate bacterial and plant-based (phytoextraction) methods of extracting metals.

topics.title: C3.3 What are electrolytes and what happens during electrolysis?

outcomes.text: Describe electrolysis in terms of ions present and reactions at the electrodes.
Predict products of electrolysing molten binary ionic compounds.
Recall that metals or hydrogen form at the cathode and non-metals at the anode with inert electrodes.
Write half equations.
Explain oxidation and reduction as loss or gain of electrons and identify what is oxidised or reduced.

subtopics.title: Electrolysis in industry and in solution

outcomes.text: Explain how electrolysis extracts metals such as aluminium.
Describe competing reactions when electrolysing aqueous solutions, including oxygen, chlorine, hydrogen and metal discharge.
Describe the technique for electrolysing an aqueous salt solution.

topics.title: C3.4 Why is crude oil important as a source of new materials?

outcomes.text: Recall that crude oil is the main source of hydrocarbons and a petrochemical feedstock.
Explain modern life's reliance on hydrocarbons and that crude oil is finite.
Describe and explain fractional distillation of crude oil.
Describe fractions as mixtures of alkanes, CnH2n+2, in a homologous series.
Use energy and relative bond and intermolecular force strengths to explain different change-of-state temperatures.
Deduce empirical formulae from atom ratios, models or diagrams, and the reverse.
Use arithmetic and ratio to find empirical formulae.
Describe the arrangement of bonds in simple molecules.
Explain covalent bonding as shared electrons.
Draw dot and cross diagrams for simple covalent substances.
Represent 3-D structures of simple molecules in 2-D and the reverse.
Describe limitations of dot and cross, ball and stick, and 2-D/3-D models.
Translate information between diagrams and numbers.
Explain bulk properties of simple molecules from covalent bonds versus intermolecular forces.
Describe how cracking makes more useful materials such as petrol fuels and alkenes.
Recognise functional groups and identify members of a homologous series.
Name and draw displayed formulae of the first four alkanes, alkenes, alcohols and carboxylic acids.
Predict products of combustion, addition across a double bond, and oxidation of alcohols to carboxylic acids.
Recall that the reactions of functional groups determine the reactions of organic compounds.

topics.title: C4.1 How is data used to choose a material for a particular use?

outcomes.text: Compare quantitatively the physical properties of glass and clay ceramics, polymers, composites and metals.
Explain how material properties relate to uses and choose a material for a given use.
Describe the composition of important alloys, including steel, in relation to their properties and uses.

topics.title: C4.2 What are the different types of polymers? (separate science only)

outcomes.text: Recall the principles of addition polymerisation: the monomer's functional group and the repeating unit.
Deduce an addition polymer's structure from its monomer, and the reverse.
Explain the principles of condensation polymerisation: functional groups, repeating units and a small molecule released.
Recall that DNA is a polymer of four nucleotides and that other natural polymers are based on sugars and amino acids.

topics.title: C4.3 How do bonding and structure affect properties of materials?

outcomes.text: Explain how bulk properties relate to bond types, bond strength versus intermolecular forces, and bond arrangement.
Recall that carbon forms four covalent bonds.
Explain that carbon's ability to form chains and rings gives a vast array of organic compounds.
Describe the bonds in polymers and how they affect strength, flexibility, hardness and melting point.
Describe the bonds in giant covalent structures.
Explain the properties of diamond and graphite from their structures and bonding.
Represent 3-D structures such as carbon allotropes in 2-D and the reverse.
Compare the bonds in ionic compounds, simple molecules, giant covalent structures, polymers and metals.

topics.title: C4.4 Why are nanoparticles so useful?

outcomes.text: Compare nano dimensions with those of atoms and molecules.
Describe how surface area to volume ratio changes with particle size and affects properties.
Relate properties of nanoparticulate materials to their uses.
Explain the properties of fullerenes and graphene from their structures.
Explain risks of nanoparticles: health effects, limited data on them, and relative risks and benefits.
Estimate size and scale of atoms and nanoparticles, using nanometres.
Use standard form, ratios and surface area and volume of cubes.

topics.title: C4.5 What happens to products at the end of their useful life?

outcomes.text: Describe the conditions and process of corrosion and how barriers and sacrificial protection prevent it.
Explain oxidation and reduction as gain or loss of oxygen.
Explain oxidation and reduction as loss or gain of electrons.
Describe the principles of a life cycle assessment, including resources, energy and environmental impact at each stage.
Describe incineration, landfill, electricity generation schemes, and biodegradable versus non-biodegradable materials.
Interpret data from a life cycle assessment.
Describe how PET drinks bottles are reused and recycled and why this is viable.
Evaluate factors affecting recycling decisions for crude oil and metal ore products.

topics.title: C5.1 How are chemicals separated and tested for purity?

outcomes.text: Explain that many useful materials are formulations, mixtures in definite proportions.
Explain scientific purity versus everyday use of 'pure'.
Use melting point data to tell pure from impure substances.
Recall that chromatography uses a stationary and a mobile phase.
Interpret chromatograms and calculate Rf values.
Suggest chromatography methods to tell pure from impure substances, including paper, solvents and locating agents.
Describe filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation and fractional distillation.
Suggest suitable purification techniques from information about the substances.

topics.title: C5.2 How do chemists find the composition of unknown samples? (separate science only)

outcomes.text: Describe the purpose of representative sampling in qualitative analysis.
Interpret flame tests for lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium and copper ions.
Describe the flame test technique.
Describe tests and results for calcium, copper, iron(II), iron(III) and zinc ions with sodium hydroxide.
Describe tests and results for carbonate, chloride, bromide, iodide and sulfate ions.
Interpret emission spectroscopy results against a reference set.
Describe the advantages of instrumental methods: sensitivity, accuracy and speed.
Interpret charts, especially in spectroscopy.

topics.title: C5.3 How are the amounts of substances in reactions calculated?

subtopics.title: Conservation of mass and formula mass

outcomes.text: Recall and use the law of conservation of mass.
Explain observed mass changes in non-enclosed systems using the particle model.
Calculate relative formula masses, including within a balanced equation.
Recall and use the definitions of the Avogadro constant and the mole.
Convert between mass and moles using the relative formula mass.
Deduce stoichiometry from masses and explain the effect of a limiting reactant.
Use balanced equations to calculate masses of reactants or products.
Use arithmetic, ratio, percentage and multistep calculations in quantitative chemistry.
Calculate with standard form using the Avogadro constant.
Change the subject of an equation.
Calculate theoretical product mass from a reactant mass (separate science only).
Calculate percentage yield (separate science only).
Suggest reasons for low yields (separate science only).
Relate moles of gas to volume using 24 dm3 at room temperature and pressure, and calculate gas volumes in reactions (separate science only).

topics.title: C5.4 How are the amounts of chemicals in solution measured?

outcomes.text: Tell qualitative from quantitative analysis (separate science only).
Calculate concentration in g/dm3 from solute mass and volume.
Calculate concentration in mol/dm3 from moles of solute and volume.
Describe neutralisation as acid plus alkali giving a salt plus water, for common laboratory acids and alkalis.
Recall that acids form hydrogen ions and alkalis contain hydroxide ions.
Generalise neutralisation as hydrogen ions reacting with hydroxide ions to form water.
Describe and explain the titration procedure for precise, accurate, valid and repeatable results.
Evaluate the quality of titration data.
Relate volumes and concentrations of solutions that react completely (separate science only).

topics.title: C6.1 What useful products can be made from acids?

subtopics.title: Reactions of acids and making salts

outcomes.text: Recall that acids react with some metals and with carbonates, and predict products with equations.
Describe practical procedures for making salts using filtration, evaporation, crystallisation and drying.
Use common ion formulae to deduce compound formulae.
Recall that pH measures relative acidity and alkalinity, using universal indicator and pH meters.
Use and explain dilute, concentrated, weak and strong for acids, including reactivity differences.
Use the idea that a tenfold rise in hydrogen ion concentration lowers pH by one.
Describe neutrality, acidity and alkalinity by hydrogen ion concentration and whole-number pH.

topics.title: C6.2 How do chemists control the rate of reactions?

outcomes.text: Describe how temperature, concentration, pressure and surface area change rate of reaction.
Explain effects of temperature, concentration and pressure through collision frequency and energy.
Explain the effect of particle size using surface area to volume ratio.
Describe the characteristics of catalysts and their effect on rate.
Identify catalysts in reactions.
Explain catalytic action through lower activation energy.
Suggest methods for measuring rate: gas volume, mass change, colour change and precipitate formation.
Interpret rate of reaction graphs.
Interpret graphs of reaction conditions versus rate (separate science only).
Use arithmetic and ratios when measuring rates.
Draw and interpret graphs from data to find rate.
Find gradients of graphs as a measure of rate.
Use proportionality when comparing factors affecting rate.
Describe enzymes as catalysts in living systems and some industrial processes.

topics.title: C6.3 What factors affect the yield of chemical reactions?

outcomes.text: Recall that some reactions are reversible and, in closed systems, do not reach 100% yield.
Recall that dynamic equilibrium is when forward and reverse rates are equal.
Predict how concentration, temperature and pressure shift equilibrium and choose conditions for a product, including catalysts and extremes.

topics.title: C6.4 How are chemicals made on an industrial scale? (separate science only)

outcomes.text: Recall the importance of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium compounds in agriculture.
Explain the importance, benefits and costs of the Haber process and fertilisers, including eutrophication.
Explain Haber process conditions in terms of raw materials, energy, equilibrium, rate, and recycling.
Explain the trade-off between rate of production and equilibrium position.
Define atom economy.
Calculate atom economy from a balanced equation.
Use arithmetic when calculating atom economy.
Explain why a reaction pathway is chosen using atom economy, yield, rate, equilibrium and by-products, and judge sustainability.
Describe industrial fertiliser production as several integrated processes, with flow charts, by-products and continuous production.
Compare industrial fertiliser production with laboratory synthesis.
